Someone only tuning into their first Red Sox game of the season Saturday might not understand the significance of Brayan Bello’s dominant performance against the hosting Tampa Bay Rays.
Particularly as it will be forever marred by a Rays’ 2-1 walk-off victory that keeps Boston’s postseason ticket dangling out of reach for at least another night.
But before that frustrating ending, there was Bello’s hard-earned triumph. It has been a tumultuous year for the homegrown right-hander, who lost his spot in the Red Sox starting rotation at the beginning of May, and pitched his way into a Triple-A demotion the first week of June. Bello dominated in a bulk-relief role from his mid-July recall through early September before the Red Sox gave him another chance to start.
Making his second start of the month on Saturday, Bello turned in not only his best game of the season, but one of the best of his five-year career. He owned his team’s first-place division rivals for eight innings of one-run ball. He yielded just five hits, issued no walks and matched his career-high 11 strikeouts.
“That was exceptional,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters postgame. “By far and away his best outing of the year. As good as I’ve seen him. So, I don’t know what else to say. He was awesome, really awesome.”
Bello’s reward was a no-decision, as the Red Sox lineup went 1 for 11 with runners in scoring position, then lost on Rays second baseman Richie Palacios’ walk-off RBI single in the bottom of the ninth.
Palacios’ game-winning hit came moments after a base-running gamble by Red Sox third baseman Caleb Durbin that proved calamitous. A glimmer of hope flared when Durbin collected his second double of the day, off Bryan Baker with one out in the top of the ninth. But he was then caught trying to steal third, which proved costly almost instantaneously when Jarren Duran tripled on the very next pitch. Isiah Kiner-Falefa’s inning-ending groundout sent the tie game to the bottom of the ninth.
“I’m OK with it,” Tracy said of Durbin’s attempt to steal. “It’s one-to-one game the whole way, and close play.”
“Hindsight is 20/20,” Tracy continued. “It’s easy in baseball. He gets thrown out, and then Duran has a triple. But you don’t have the privilege of hindsight. So (Durbin) was working hard out there, seeing if he can get the bag, and they got him.”
“I thought I had a window, and probably wasn’t a big enough window,” Durbin told reporters. “I those situations, too, you want to be sure about it. So obviously on me. Not really any excuse other than I gotta be more sure.”
Roman Anthony gave the Red Sox an early lead for the second straight game, doubling off Rays starter Freddy Peralta with two outs in the third. Anthony’s third RBI base hit of the series scored Durbin, who led off the frame with his first double.
But that was all the Red Sox wrote. The home team peppered the middle innings with costly mistakes, but the visitors never took advantage.
Rays centerfielder Cedric Mullins reached safely on a bunt single and advanced to second on a throwing error by Durbin to begin the bottom of the third, but Boston’s third baseman immediately atoned for the miscue by completing a caught-stealing relay with catcher Adley Rutschman and shortstop Trevor Story.
Tampa Bay ran out of ABS challenges by the fourth inning. Shortstop Jorge Mateo burned one on a called Strike 3 from Bello (1.2” Edge Distance) for the second out of the bottom of the third. Peralta lost his team’s remaining bid trying to overturn a Ball 4 with a 2.8” Edge Distance, which put right-fielder Wilyer Abreu on with one out in the fourth.
The worm turned in the bottom of the fourth. Boston’s squandering of a one-out opportunity with Abreu and Nick Sogard (single) on first and second in the top of the inning proved costly immediately when Jonathan Aranda led off the bottom with a first-pitch, game-tying home run.
An undeterred Bello held fast to the knot inning after inning, and looked effortless doing so. Whereas Peralta exited after 5 2/3 innings that required 97 pitches (59 for strikes), Bello needed 55 pitches to complete the first five frames, and his count sat at 68 at the end of the sixth.
When the Rays finally threatened in the bottom of the seventh, the Sox starter was the picture of poise. Unruffled by the back-to-back singles by Liam Hicks and Chandler Simpson, Bello retired the next three men in order. The game became his longest of the season as a starter or reliever when he recorded the first out of the seventh, and when he returned to the dugout after finishing the eighth inning, it marked his deepest outing since his complete game on July 8, 2025.
With closer Aroldis Chapman still unavailable due to lat tightness, it fell to righty Garrett Whitlock to pitch the game to extra innings. Whitlock was one strike away from stranding slugger Junior Caminero and Simpson when Palacios sent his 1-2 sinker to right field, where it plunked down in front of Abreu.
The loss means Sunday is the earliest the Red Sox can punch their ticket to October. The current playoff picture has the Red Sox and Yankees meeting in a rematch of last year’s best-of-three Wild Card series at Yankee Stadium. If Boston gets beyond that, they could see Tampa Bay again.
Saturday’s intensity felt like a preview to the Red Sox. Durbin hopes they can turn the experience into an advantage.
“That was a hell of a baseball game,” Tracy said. “I don’t have really anything negative to say about that game, other than it was really well-played on both sides by both teams. Big moments, and people rose the occasion. It was just a heck of a baseball game, and they were able to beat us.”
“Even yesterday and tomorrow, like they got a little bit of a playoff feel,” Durbin said. “I feel like last year (with the Milwaukee Brewers), first couple playoff games … adrenaline’s way higher. So to get that feel before playoffs even start is super important, because it usually takes a couple games to really settle in. So if we could settle in by Game 1 or 2, that’ll be big for us.”

There's a version of this continuous Boston Red Sox news saga that could have sent fans into a real panic, and I get why. Justin Slaten had quietly turned into one of the more trustworthy arms in this bullpen, working to a 2.84 ERA over his final two months of availability before elbow trouble sidelined him in August.
Now we know the full picture: an evaluation revealed degenerative changes in the flexor mass of his right elbow, and rather than push for a return with the postseason approaching, the Red Sox are having him get a PRP injection and start planning for 2027 instead.
On the year, he had thirty-six appearances, a 4.60 ERA overall, but provided a real chunk of high-leverage relief work, which is now gone for the stretch run. That's a real hole, absolutely. It's also not the whole story right now, and it's worth taking a breath before assuming the bullpen just got worse.
Garrett Crochet was the AL Cy Young runner-up last season, an 18-5, 2.59 ERA workhorse who threw 205.1 innings and struck out 255 batters. What a lot of people forget is that before all of that, Crochet broke into pro ball as a reliever with the Chicago White Sox, sitting comfortably in the upper 90s and regularly touching triple digits in short bursts. That's exactly the version the Red Sox may get back down the stretch.
He hasn't pitched in a game since throwing six scoreless innings on April 25, and after months sidelined with a shoulder issue that turned into more of a lingering problem, he just threw his first bullpen sessions in nearly three months. There isn't time left to stretch him back out as a starter, but a Crochet who can air it out for one to three innings at a time is exactly the profile that's thrived in October before.
Pair that with a Payton Tolle start going five or six innings, Crochet bridging the seventh and eighth, and Aroldis Chapman closing it out, and that's a real, dangerous alignment behind Sonny Gray in a Game 1.
Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo are trending toward returns to Red Sox bullpen alongside Garrett Crochet
Crochet isn't walking through that door alone, either. Tanner Houck is further along than anyone, working back from UCL surgery and already up to three innings and 48 pitches in a rehab outing for Double-A Portland, allowing just one run with four strikeouts, before moving on to Triple-A Worcester to keep building and facing some better competition.
Johan Oviedo, who Boston acquired from the Pittsburgh Pirates over the winter, finally made his own rehab appearance with Worcester this week after missing more than five months with a flexor strain, which is a sign he could factor into the bullpen picture before the year is out. Kutter Crawford is the longer shot of the group, hasn't pitched for the big club since 2024, and there are only unconfirmed "rumblings" he could get a look at Worcester this week. Even if that goes nowhere in 2026, he's still under team control for two more seasons.
Losing Slaten hurts, and nobody should pretend otherwise. But between Crochet, Houck, and Oviedo all trending in the right direction at the same time, Boston may be walking into the stretch run with more usable, high-upside arms than it's had healthy at any single point all season.

On the verge of clinching a postseason berth for the second straight year, the Boston Red Sox have reason to be cautiously optimistic about the health of one of their best hitters.
Though still “pretty sore” from taking a pitch to the right hand on Sept. 17, Willson Contreras no longer believes he suffered a fracture, because he woke up feeling better and had improved range of motion and grip.
“I’m not concerned about having a fracture, just because I can squeeze a lot better today,” the All-Star first baseman told reporters before the team’s Saturday afternoon game at the Tampa Bay Rays’ Tropicana Field. “I had a fracture in my right hand in 2024 by hit-by-pitch, and I couldn’t squeeze at all.”
“But it’s going to take days,” Contreras cautioned.
Contreras’ 24th hit-by-pitch of the season, a 92.3 mph sinker from Rangers’ Jakob Junis to his knuckle in the eighth inning, was a moment of extreme panic for him and the team. Contreras initially went to take his base, but was evidently in severe pain and interim manager Chad Tracy and athletic trainer Dave Herrera quickly removed him from the game.
Though initial imaging was negative, Contreras and Tracy both acknowledged the swelling could be obscurative, with the former telling reporters postgame, “It felt like a fracture.”
“When I got hit, I felt my hand going numb, and I thought it was bad, because that’s a sign of a fracture,” Contreras said on Saturday. “And it was like, tingling for like five minutes.”
Contreras will try to grip a bat on Sunday, and if so, try to do some cage work. He is champing at the bit to get back in games before the postseason begins. He has soared to new heights in his 11th big-league season and first with the Red Sox, putting up career-best marks in his .905 OPS, 59 walks, 81 RBI, and 27 home runs (129 games).
“I’m dying to go out and play with the guys and be there for them,” Contreras said. “It’s part of baseball; I’ll do everything in my power to get back on the field.”
“You don’t want to get to the playoffs without playing any games,” he said. “I want to do everything in my power to get back on the field before the playoffs. If it happens, it happens. If it doesn’t happen, we’ll see what happens.”
Contreras is one of several injured stars the Red Sox are eager to have back as they careen toward October baseball. Gold Glove centerfielder Ceddanne Rafaela last played Sept. 2 before going on the injured list with a right quad strain. Though it’s unlikely Rafaela will get into a Triple-A Worcester game before their season ends on Sunday, interim manager Chad Tracy described him as “moving quickly in the right direction,” and said the goal is for him to get “live BP-type at-bats of some kind, plus the Trajekt (pitching machine).”
All-Star closer Aroldis Chapman is not on the IL, but remains day-to-day due to the lat tightness he felt during a workout before Tuesday’s game in Texas. Though unavailable for this weekend’s series in Tampa, he told reporters there (through a team translator), “I’m not worried at all. … I feel very good. I was going to go out and throw, but the team wants to take it slow, and they want me to take my time.” Chapman plans to get back in games during the team’s final homestand, which begins Tuesday versus the Cleveland Guardians.

Sep 19, 2026, 11:07 AM ET
Boston Red Sox left-handed closer Aroldis Chapman (lat) felt some tightness in his lat while working out before Tuesday's game against the Texas Rangers and has not pitched since. Chapman said that he will not pitch this weekend against the division-rival Tampa Bay Rays, but he expects to return during the final homestand of the regular season, which starts on Tuesday, according to Ian Browne of MLB.com. The veteran southpaw downplayed the injury on Friday, saying that the Red Sox are being conservative and that he felt healthy enough to play catch before the series opener against the Rays, but the team told him not to. "I'm not worried at all," Chapman said. "From the first time I felt it to today, I feel very good. I was going to go out and throw, but the team wants to take it slow, and they want me to take my time." Fantasy managers will be without Chapman this weekend, but for championship matchups next week, he will hopefully be ready to return to ninth-inning duties. The 38-year-old has been excellent in 2026 in his second year in Boston, posting a 1.95 ERA with a 1.14 WHIP, 34 saves, and 68 strikeouts in 50 2/3 innings pitched. Right-hander Garrett Whitlock should handle a save situation this weekend if it arises in Tampa.--Keith Hernandez

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — When Roman Anthony returned to the Boston Red Sox three weeks ago after nearly four months on the injury list with a torn right finger ligament, it initially looked as if he had barely missed any time.
Through his first five games after he was activated Aug. 30 in New York, Anthony recorded four games with multiple hits, going 10-for-22 with two homers, two doubles and a triple. His methodical rehab, missing 101 games, paid dividends with a bat that was ready to perform.
Advertisement
But then, as so often happens in baseball, he fell out of rhythm at the plate, collecting just seven hits, including just one extra-base hit, in his next 56 plate appearances.
That’s why he found himself in an early batting practice session Friday afternoon with hitting coach John Soteropulos, tinkering in the cage with a few mechanical adjustments.
The work clicked.
Oh baby, Roman! pic.twitter.com/aP7bBEgZX0
— Red Sox (@RedSox) September 18, 2026
Three pitches into the game, Anthony clubbed a solo homer for a lead, and in the second inning, he smacked a bases-loaded single to drive in two more runs as the Red Sox beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-2, snapping the Rays’ six-game win streak. The win inched the Red Sox closer to clinching a playoff berth. A Red Sox win Saturday, coupled with a Texas Rangers loss, would punch Boston’s ticket to the playoffs.
“We came out and looked really good offensively in the first part of that game, and there was a lot of energy in the dugout,” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “I think guys feel it. We’re not done yet, but I definitely think they sniff it, and we’re wanting to get there for sure.”
With eight games left in the regular season, getting Anthony’s bat hot again, particularly as Willson Contreras remains day to day with a deeply bruised right hand, will be imperative for the Red Sox lineup in the postseason.
“He will,” Tracy said confidently about Anthony’s bat regaining momentum. “I mean, you see what he can do. It’s the game of baseball, there’s ebbs and flows. He came off the rehab, and for like five games, he looked fantastic. Then he went through some stuff, and now he’s starting to look good again. When he’s going well, you see the impact he can make.”
Before Soteropulos was elevated to lead hitting coach this season after an overhaul of the coaching staff, he was the minor-league hitting coordinator and worked closely with Anthony. That relationship has helped.
Advertisement
“Me and John have been working on some things, really since I have been back,” Anthony said. “He’s amazing. He’s somebody who knows my swing so well. We have been together since I came into this org, all throughout the minor leagues. Having somebody here, somebody who knows my swing and when to talk and when to tinker. Nobody knows me better than John.
“It’s such a constant game of adjustments and looking over a span of my last few at-bats, it obviously was not where I wanted to be. I was hitting the ball on the ground, to the right side, so I was trying to get away from that. Hitting early on the field with John and with Trevor (Story) definitely helped.”
Anthony’s first-inning homer came off the bat at an estimated 107.7 mph with an estimated distance of 438 feet, marking the longest homer of his career.
But to him, the two-run single was just as important. In a rough series in Texas, the Red Sox had gone just 1-for-18 with runners in scoring position. His goal was to alleviate some pressure on the offense by simply making contact.
“That’s my job, to do everything I can to put the ball in play and find ways on base,” he said. “That’s how I have had a lot of success in the past as a leadoff hitter. So over these last games, just keep putting an emphasis on being the best leadoff hitter I can be. See as many pitches I can and try and get on base. It was a huge way to start the game. This game is all about momentum, so any time you can get something like that going, it’s huge.”
The two-run single gave the Red Sox the lead back after the Rays tied the score off Ranger Suarez in the bottom of the first. Jahmai Jones made it 4-1 in the third with his sixth homer of the year.
The insurance gave the Red Sox a cushion as Suarez was uncharacteristically spotty with command, walking a career-high five batters.
Advertisement
Still, he navigated traffic in each of the first four innings and allowed just the one run on three hits in 5 2/3 innings. Reliever Wyatt Olds wiggled out of a jam in the sixth after Suarez exited, walking two batters to load the bases, then falling behind pinch hitter Jake Fraley 3-1. Olds came back to strike out Fraley.
The Red Sox faced more trouble in the ninth, with reliever Erik Miller still searching for his command. Closer Aroldis Chapman remains day to day with lat tightness, and Tracy turned to Miller for the ninth with Garrett Whitlock having a heavy load of late.
Miller allowed a run in the ninth on an infield single, a wild pitch, a walk and a groundout. He loaded the bases after a strikeout got away on a wild pitch, but escaped the jam with a groundout to close it out.
Clinching their postseason spot with a week left in the regular season would allow the Red Sox to breathe and reset some players before the postseason. But they’re not there yet. Saturday awaits.
“It just kind of felt like a playoff game,” Anthony said. “Getting into that mode is huge from an at-bat standpoint and from a big-game standpoint of constantly being the next man up.”

Boston Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy knows his team has figured out the Tampa Bay Rays pretty well this season.
That said, the Red Sox (84-70) still can learn more about the Rays (93-60) when the teams meet Saturday afternoon in St. Petersburg, Fla.
"At this point with (the Rays), we've played them enough already," Tracy said. "We have a pretty good understanding of them, (and) they have a pretty good understanding of us. But you could always pick up more stuff."
In Friday's series opener, the Red Sox scored four runs over the first three innings and won 4-2 to snap Tampa Bay's six-game winning streak and improve to 6-5 this season vs. the Rays.
Boston currently holds the second wild-card position in the American League but is dealing with several injuries.
"We have guys beat up that aren't here, and the hope is we get people healthy, and the roster could look even different a week from now than it does right now," Tracy said.
Boston's Willson Contreras is day-to-day after getting hit on the hand, while closer Aroldis Chapman (lat tightness) has been unavailable the past two contests.
Right-hander Tanner Houck (Tommy John surgery in 2025) and lefty Garrett Crochet (left shoulder inflammation) have advanced in their rehab assignments.
Boston left-hander Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.02 ERA) is expected to make his 26th start on Saturday and will try to record his sixth consecutive win.
Tolle is 1-0 with an 0.75 ERA over 12 innings in his last two starts, allowing one run on eight hits while striking out 19 with a walk. He is 0-2 with a 4.50 ERA in two starts and one relief outing against Tampa Bay, which already has clinched a playoff berth.
Whatever Rays pitching coach Kyle Snyder and the rest of the staff have done with trade-deadline acquisition Freddy Peralta certainly has been a success.
Acquired by the club from the New York Mets for three prospects on Aug. 2, Peralta (9-11, 4.67 ERA) -- a right-hander who will start for the Rays on Saturday -- arrived from the Big Apple as a lesser version of what he was during his two All-Star seasons with the Milwaukee Brewers.
He was 5-9 with a 4.99 ERA with the Mets, but the work was immediately put in by the Rays to adjust Peralta to where he was when he was a 17-game winner with a sub-3.00 ERA last season.
"For some reason, when I got here, when I sat here with Kyle and (bullpen coach Jorge Moncada) and (manager Kevin Cash), they told me, like, 'You're gonna do what you want to do here, and we are going to help you to do it,'" Peralta said.
"And we know what you need to do to make those adjustments. We just put everything on the table. I just followed all the instructions, and it's what I am right now."
With the Rays, Peralta is 4-2 with a 3.86 ERA in eight starts, but his past four outings have been gems. He has pitched 23 innings and has allowed just two runs on 10 hits, with 17 strikeouts, four walks and an 0.78 ERA in that span.
"Fastball Freddy," who is using his changeup much more with the Rays, is 0-2 with a 5.40 ERA in three career starts against Boston.
Peralta allowed two runs on three hits in 4 1/3 innings in a 4-0 loss at Boston on July 11 while with the Mets.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Tampa Bay Rays have been the best team in the American League for much of this season, particularly at Tropicana Field.
But with one All-Star on the injured list and two others unavailable, the Red Sox came away with a 4-2 victory before a crowd of 23,342 as Roman Anthony drove in three runs.
Now the magic number to clinch a playoff spot is down to two.
Ranger Suarez (8-4) and three relievers walked nine but held the Rays to five hits. Tampa Bay was hitless in 13 at-bats with runners in scoring position and left 12 men on base.
It was an impressive victory for the Sox, considering the 93-60 Rays are close to clinching the best record in the league and home-field advantage through, at least, the American League Championship Series.
The Sox were without Ceddanne Rafaela, who isn’t expected to come off the injured list until next week. Aroldis Chapman (lat strain) and Willson Contreras (bruised right hand) were not available.
With Garrett Whitlock left in the bullpen after pitching Thursday night, the Sox used lefthander Erik Miller to get the final three outs for his first save with the team.
Miller walked two and threw three wild pitches in a wild ninth inning, giving up a run before finally getting Chandler Simpson to ground to second for the final out.
Miller had allowed five runs over 5⅓ innings and put 10 men on base in his previous six appearances.
The Sox didn’t arrive at the team hotel until close to 5 a.m. after beating the Rangers in Texas on Thursday night. The Rays had a day game at home that ended 13 hours earlier. But the Sox had more energy early on.
Anthony blasted the third pitch of the game from Ian Seymour 438 feet to center field for his fifth home run.
Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin led off the second inning with singles. Isiah Kiner-Falefa dropped a bunt to advance the runners before Nate Eaton worked a walk to load the bases.
After Connor Wong struck out, Anthony worked the count full and lined a hard single to right field to drive in two more runs. The three RBIs matched his career high.
Jahmai Jones homered leading off the third inning, a 414-foot shot to left field.
Suarez did not handle the run support very well. He walked a hitter in each of the first four innings and threw 69 pitches. But the Rays scored only one run.
Yandy Diaz walked leading off the bottom of the first, advanced to third on a double by Jonathan Aranda, and scored on Junior Caminero’s groundout.
Suarez was done after 5⅔ innings and 98 pitches, leaving the game with a runner at second. Wyatt Olds walked Liam Hicks and Victor Mesa Jr. on 12 pitches to load the bases.
He fell behind Jake Fraley 3 and 1, then came back to strike him out swinging through a fastball at the top of the strike zone. Olds threw up his hands after finally ending the inning. It wasn’t an elegant outing, but it was ultimately an effective one.
Greg Weissert worked around a two-out double by Caminero in the seventh inning to keep the lead at three runs, then came back for a 1-2-3 eighth.

item.content:encoded:
Back in late June when the Red Sox sunk to their lowest depths, the idea that the club might still have a shot at reaching the postseason would have seemed hopelessly optimistic.
Yet, here they are with a little over a week left to play in the regular season, and the Red Sox have all but punched their ticket to the playoffs.
With their 4-2 win over the Tampa Bay Rays in Friday’s series opener, the Red Sox can now clinch a playoff spot as soon as Saturday. The club’s magic number, which stood at three entering the night, will drop to either one or two depending on the outcome of Friday’s late game between the Rangers and Blue Jays.
A Rangers win would mean the Red Sox could clinch with a win on Saturday, while a Blue Jays win would necessitate a win and a Blue Jays loss.
Following a string of poor offensive performances, Friday got off to a much stronger start at the plate. Roman Anthony put the Red Sox in front with a solo home run to lead off the game, and after the Rays tied it up in the bottom half of the first, Anthony delivered again in the second with a go-ahead two-run single with the bases loaded off Rays starter Ian Seymour, an alumnus of St. John’s High School in Shrewsbury.
Anthony finished 2 for 4 with three RBI, and the Red Sox never looked back.
“Taking that first one is big,” Anthony told NESN’s Jahmai Webster postgame. “Any win you can get against a team like that it’s a great win, so it’s a great day.”
Anthony’s first-inning blast was smoked. Measured at 107.7 mph off the bat and traveling 438 feet, the solo home run to right field narrowly missed landing in Tropicana Field’s ray tank.
His two-run single in the second inning was hit even harder, coming off the bat at 108.7 mph. Anthony came through after Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin led off the inning with singles, Isiah Kiner-Falefa moved them into scoring position with a sacrifice bunt and Nate Eaton walked to load the bases.
It was doubly encouraging given Anthony’s recent struggles at the plate. After a hot start coming off the injured list, the outfielder came into Friday batting just .137 with one extra base hit over his past 12 games.
“I’ve been grinding, but that’s the beauty of this team,” Anthony said. “You’re never down and you’re never out.”
Jahmai Jones capped off the early offense with a solo shot to lead off the top of the third.
Tampa Bay scored its early run in the first after Yandy Diaz drew a leadoff walk, advanced to third on a Jonathan Aranda double and scored on a Junior Caminero groundout. But that was all the damage the Rays could do against Ranger Suarez, who allowed one run over 5 2/3 innings while falling one out short of his third consecutive quality start.
Suarez was uncharacteristically wild, walking five batters, but he limited the damage by allowing just three hits while striking out five.
The walks almost cost the Red Sox in the sixth inning.
Still leading by three, Suarez issued his fifth and final walk to lead off the sixth before recording two quick outs to finish his outing. But Wyatt Olds came on and immediately walked the first two men he faced, loading the bases and bringing the go-ahead run to the plate.
A brief mound visit followed, and Olds dug deep and struck out pinch hitter Jake Fraley to escape the inning unscathed.
“It was a weird game all the way around, we walked nine in total, Ranger walked five but still almost completed six innings and he was very competitive with men on base,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in St. Petersburg. “He lost some counts and behind more counts today, but he was able to make really good pitches with people on base.”
Walks put the Red Sox in one more jam in the bottom of the ninth inning.
With Aroldis Chapman unavailable with a lat issue and Garrett Whitlock having pitched on Thursday, Erik Miller took the mound in the ninth and walked three men. He allowed a run to score on a Victor Mesa Jr. groundout, and the third walk to Caminero brought the winning run to the plate with two outs.
Miller struck out Ryan Vilade, but the ball got away from Connor Wong and the Rays batter reached safely to extend the game and load the bases. But Miller fought back and drew a game-ending groundout from Chandler Simpson, leaving the Rays 0 for 13 with runners in scoring position and 12 men left on base in spite of the nine walks issued by the Red Sox pitching staff.
While Miller has now walked seven batters over his last 3 1/3 innings, Tracy said he felt the left-hander looked much better on Friday despite all of the traffic.
“I thought he was way more competitive,” Tracy said. “Everything was around the zone, stuff was good, he was getting some swing and miss like he usually does so I take a lot of good out of that outing.”
The win marked Boston’s first at Tropicana Field this season, and the club hopes plenty more will follow in the days and weeks to come. The Rays have long been in the driver’s seat for the AL East title, and barring a complete collapse over the final week Tampa Bay should soon lock down the American League’s top seed and a bye to the divisional round.
That means if the Red Sox (84-70) can get past the Yankees in the AL Wild Card Series, they’d be headed right back to St. Petersburg to face the Rays in a rematch of the 2021 ALDS.
But first, the Red Sox hope to pop some bottles in the Tropicana Field visitor’s clubhouse before they fly back to Boston. First pitch on Saturday is scheduled for 4:10 p.m.

ST. PETERSBURG – As they head into the final 10 days of the regular season, the Red Sox are monitoring a plethora of injuries to key players.
Given that the Sox still hold firm possession of the second American League Wild Card spot and could clinch a berth as early as this weekend, the plan will be to operate conservatively in hopes of getting everyone healthy for the games that count the most.
Here is an update on where things stand with those key players.
First baseman Willson Contreras
There was a big scare on Thursday night in Texas when the team’s most productive hitter this season was pelted on the top of his right hand with a pitch in the top of the eighth and immediately exited the game. Contreras said that in the moment, it felt like a fracture. Fortunately, X-rays taken at the ballpark were negative.
While interim manager Chad Tracy mentioned the possibility of follow-up imaging, there was none on Friday. Contreras didn’t have his hand taped and spent his share of time in the training room.
Where do things stand?
“Obviously, sore with some swelling,” Tracy said. “So nothing new other than just over the next couple of days, they'll work on treatment, on getting the swelling out, see if he can get grip strength back, and then we'll go from there. So just day to day.”
Could there still be additional scans?
“Not right now. Right now, with the initial one, they're optimistic,” said Tracy. “Just work on the swelling and see how he progresses over the next couple days, and then determine if they feel like they need more. But right now, they're just going to work on that.”
Closer Aroldis Chapman
When Garrett Whitlock closed Thursday’s win in Texas, it was obvious something was up with Chapman. It turns out he has been dealing with lat tightness he sustained while working out prior to Tuesday’s game.
Chapman downplayed the injury on Friday, saying the team is being conservative and that he felt healthy enough to play catch before the opener of the three-game series against the Rays. The Red Sox told him not to.
The lefty fireballer said he won’t pitch this weekend, but he expects to return during the final homestand, which starts on Tuesday.
“I’m not worried at all,” Chapman said. “From the first time I felt it to today, I feel very good. I was going to go out and throw, but the team wants to take it slow, and they want me to take my time.“
It is all about being 100% for the first game of the playoffs on Sept. 29, right?
“Yeah, of course,” said Chapman. “A hundred percent.”
Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela
Boston’s All-Star center fielder hasn’t played since Sept. 2 due to a right quad strain. It sounds unlikely he’ll be able to play in a rehab game for Triple-A Worcester because that season ends on Sunday. But Tracy is confident with where Rafaela is at.
“I think he got close to 90% of his acceleration yesterday,” said Tracy. “So not ready yet, but he's moving quickly in the right direction, which is good. If he doesn’t play [for Worcester], there is a goal of getting him some live at-bats of some kind. You know, like live BP-type at-bats of some kind, plus the Trajekt. The important thing is that the running piece keeps going in the right direction.”
Left-hander Garrett Crochet
Boston’s ace, who has been out since April 25 due to a left shoulder injury, is still racing against the clock to try to pitch in relief during the postseason. His next step will be on Saturday, when he throws his second up-and-down bullpen session of the week at Fenway Park.
For Crochet to have any shot at pitching at the start of the postseason, he would have to start facing hitters by next week.
“I would say we're to the point where these next five days or so are going to be pretty telling,” said Tracy. “How does the side go, and what can we do with him early next week? And that'll give us a better idea of the answer to that question.”
Right-hander Tanner Houck
The righty will make the fourth and final appearance of his Minor League rehab assignment when he throws roughly 50 pitches for Worcester on Saturday. It’s possible Houck will get a tuneup or two in regular-season action for the Red Sox next week, which could give the club a better gauge if he’s a possibility to pitch in the playoffs. Houck had Tommy John surgery 13 months ago.

Willson Contreras played a key role in the Boston Red Sox's come-from-behind win in the series finale against the Texas Rangers, but not in a way he would have preferred. Contreras was plunked in the hand by struggling Rangers reliever Jakob Junis in the top of the eighth, setting the scene for Trevor Story to launch a go-ahead three-run homer off All-Star closer Jacob Latz.
The good news is that Contreras underwent x-rays following the game, and they came back clean. The veteran didn't seem to agree with the diagnosis, saying that it felt like a fracture and that he's fractured that hand before and experienced some numbness. More importantly, he's frustrated.
“If nobody does anything about it, I’m going to keep getting hit. That’s the way I see it. That’s it,” Contreras said, via Tim Healey of The Boston Globe.
Contreras has been hit by a pitch 24 times this season, third-most in the league. Of course, he also crowds the plate more than almost any hitter in the game. You want to claim the entire plate as your own; expect opposing pitchers to try and prove to you that the inside corner is, in fact, theirs.
By the sound of it, that is lost on Contreras. It seems as if the former St. Louis Cardinal wants one of Boston's pitchers to go out and start beaning batters in retaliation. That might be how things were done in the olden days, but now that's a recipe for escalation, a potential brawl, and possible suspensions.
Given that he doesn't feel as if any of the hurlers have come to his defense, it's likely that won't change. These bad feelings could become a cause for concern, and even more so with us approaching October's doorstep.
Willson Contreras could be threatening Red Sox chemistry again with latest HBP outrage
On the field, Contreras has had a fantastic first season in Boston. His 27 homers are already a career high, and if it holds, his .387 on-base percentage will be a career-best, too. Meanwhile, his .518 slugging percentage is the second-best mark of his career. There was a reason why he was voted a top AL MVP contender in an MLB.com poll at the end of August.
That's been great, but there have been issues. Contreras made some confusing comments after Alex Cora was dismissed, seemingly taking a shot at the team's young players in the process. He has also gotten into it with fans after being booed for not running out a ground ball back in August, further cementing his reputation as a prickly player.
At the same time, before the tide turned on the Red Sox's season and trade rumors enveloped him, he stated that he wouldn't waive his no-trade clause, desiring to finish his career in Boston.
Overall, it's odd. At times, it has seemed as if he doesn't really want to be here, despite his protest that, in fact, Boston is the only place he envisions himself playing.
This latest incident is more dangerous. Who knows what is said behind closed doors, but hurt bodies and hurt feelings don't go well together. If Contreras pushes the "defense" issue, it could cause a real rift. The pitchers could side with each other, while the hitters rally around Contreras.
The lines could also be different if there are enough players on either side of the positional divide with a more updated view of bean ball, so that different cliques could form.
The Red Sox have bigger issues at hand right now. They're going to have to figure out their postseason roster crunch. They're hoping that Aroldis Chapman's sore lat isn't anything serious. They need to find a way to get Roman Anthony's bat going before the playoffs begin. What they don't have time for is Contreras getting in his feelings because he got hit while standing on top of the plate.

Boston Red Sox fans were already going through it on Thursday night after Willson Contreras left the series finale against the Texas Rangers early after being hit by a pitch on the hand. Seeing Garrett Whitlock emerge from the bullpen to close a 4-3 game in the ninth inning only made fears worse.
Whitlock is no slouch, as Red Sox fans know, and he got through the ninth frame unscathed, but fans expect to see Aroldis Chapman in moments like that. After the game, Boston announced that Chapman was unavailable due to a lat issue.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said in his September 17 postgame presser that Chapman has been dealing with lat tightness for a couple of days but that he's been improving lately. Boston has classified him as day-to-day and it will routinely check on his recovery progress to gauge his availability.
The best news from Tracy on Chapman is that the team will not place him on the injured list. The Sox's bullpen has been one of their deadliest weapons all season and Chapman with his 1.95 ERA, 34 saves, blistering velocity and unmatched consistency at 38 years old has been a huge part of that success.
Aroldis Chapman injury news is a blow the Red Sox's bullpen can't afford as the playoffs near
Still, having Chapman at anything less than 100 percent is dangerous this late in the season with the playoffs on the horizon. In a tight game, one slip-up in the ninth inning could lead to disaster.
The rest of the Red Sox's bullpen is hardly in its best shape. Justin Slaten's season ended following continued flexor issues and Tyron Guerrero is still on the IL bouncing back from shoulder inflammation. Erik Miller is also dealing with a mechanical issue that has severely impacted his command over his last two outings.
If Chapman's injury is as mild as Tracy is letting on and he doesn't need an IL stint, Boston might be able to avoid disaster. But it also needs Chapman's help to clinch its playoff spot in the first place. The offense is struggling to get out to enough of a lead that it doesn't need Chapman to hold a slim margin in the late innings, but that won't fly in the postseason, especially with an injured closer.
At least the Red Sox expect some relief reinforcements in the coming days. Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet are working towards returns from long-term injuries in a relief role and they could take some pressure off the 'pen, but neither could fill Chapman's role.

Alec Gamboa, who played for the Lotte Giants in the KBO League last year. He failed to re-sign with Lotte, but a year later he debuted in the major leagues and is aiming to make the postseason roster.
On the 18th (Korean time) at Globe Life Field in Arlington, Texas, in the game against the Texas Rangers, Gamboa came in with one out in the eighth inning and no runners on, recorded 2/3 of an inning, allowed one hit and no runs, and earned a hold. It was his second hold of the season.
That day Gamboa entered the game after Trevor Story hit a go-ahead three-run homer in the top of the eighth to put them up 4-3. Starter Sonny Gray pitched well with 6 1/3 innings, three hits (one home run), three walks, six strikeouts and three runs, and second pitcher Wyatt Alls recorded one inning, one strikeout and no runs.
Gamboa came in to face a left-handed batting lineup of Corey Seager and Josh Young. He gave up a single to the first batter, Seager, to right field. Later, he fell behind Josh Young 3-1 in the count but induced a shortstop grounder with a low 95.6-mph sinker, producing a double play to end the inning.
After recording his first hold in his debut by getting Lee Jung-hoo and others out in the Aug. 22 game against the San Francisco Giants, he recorded his second hold of the season. Gamboa's season performance is excellent. In 19 appearances he pitched 29 2/3 innings with 1 win, 2 holds, 1 save, a 1.21 ERA, a .216 batting average against and a 1.04 WHIP.
That day closer Aroldis Chapman could not take the mound because of trapezius muscle stiffness, and another lefty in the high-leverage group, Eric Miller, had earlier shown instability on the 17th against Texas by allowing three runs on 22 pitches in one inning. As a result, rookie right-hander Wyatt Alls and left-hander Gamboa had to take on the high-leverage roles, and setup man Garrett Whitlock had to assume the closer role. All of them then held the one-run lead.
Acting manager Chad Tracy praised Alls and Gamboa's high-leverage performances, saying, "They were really great. They were inserted suddenly into important situations. At times they had to take the mound with the lead, and they did really well."
Gamboa once again successfully passed a high-leverage test for the high-leverage group. Now the question is whether he can join Boston's postseason journey. Boston has a 83-70 record and sits second in the wild-card standings. They are five games ahead of the third-place Cleveland Guardians, so barring an upset they are all but certain to secure the 5 seed.
Over the Monster, which reports on Boston news, listed Gamboa in the "pitchers who need to prove themselves" spot while predicting the postseason roster. The outlet said, "He is a player who had a pleasantly surprising performance this year. He even made two starts as an opener. In recent weeks the bullpen has had injuries, and combined with his own performance, he has risen to the point of being used in higher-stakes, high-leverage situations."
Closers Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Eric Miller, Tyrone Guerrero and Garrett Crochet are confirmed. It is likely that one more left-handed reliever will be added and the rest filled with right-handers.
They went on to say, "If Aroldis Chapman, Eric Miller and Garrett Crochet are the confirmed left-handed bullpen pieces, the final left-handed spot could be a competition between Hobani Moran and Gamboa," and added, "If I had to pick the final four now, I would choose Brayan Bello, Tanner Houck, Moran and Gamboa," predicting they would make the postseason roster.

Gamboa was drafted by the Los Angeles Dodgers in the ninth round, 281st overall, in the 2019 draft. But he couldn't break through the Dodgers' deep minor league system, and last year he joined the KBO League's Lotte Giants as a replacement player and delivered a sensational performance.

His KBO League stats were 19 games, 108 innings, 7 wins, 8 losses and a 3.58 ERA.

I wanted to experience a bigger and new environment than Triple-A in the U.S. I believed I would show good pitching there, return to the U.S. and seize another opportunity," and added, "Before going to Korea I had never been abroad. Experiencing another country, seeing how polite the people there are and how much they love baseball, and seeing what style of baseball they play was really fun," saying it was an opportunity that lifted his spirits.
Was failing to re-sign with Lotte a blessing in disguise? After signing a minor league deal with Boston he made an emotional big league debut and now stands on the verge of making the postseason roster. Gamboa is becoming a symbol of a life turnaround.

The New York Yankees and Boston Red Sox seem destined for another October clash. You can smell the narrative building now. The Red Sox will be painted as the underdogs due to their horrid start to the season. Fine. Whatever makes them feel better.
For the Yankees, this could be a tipping point, a chance to regain that sense of dominance over their hated rival. To that end, New York might have just gotten a piece of news that could further tip the scales in its favor, and it has to do old "friend" Aroldis Chapman.
After dropping the first two games of their series against the Texas Rangers, Boston mounted a late-inning comeback following a Trevor Story three-run homer in the eighth inning against Texas's all-world closer Jacob Latz. Coming out to secure the victory in the ninth wasn't Chapman, though; instead, it was another former Yankee, Garrett Whitlock. After the game, it was revealed that Chapman was "unavailable" because he's dealing with a sore lat.
Red Sox interim manager said that it's an issue that Chapman has been dealing with for a few days, and that the team will be conservative with his usage for the time being. The 38-year-old, who recently learned the importance of throwing strikes, has seen his command get spotty over his last two outings, issuing three walks in the process. Perhaps the injury is to blame?
Red Sox injury issues, including Aroldis Chapman, Willson Contreras, and others, could give Yankees the upper hand
At this point, it's unclear whether or not Chapman will need to head to the IL, but either way him being less than 100% bodes well for the Yankees. That will be especially true if he remains active and reverts to his wild ways in the upcoming playoff matchup.
Chapman isn't the only Boston player banged up, either. Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch on the hand during the Red Sox's win over the Rangers. X-rays were initially negative, but the former St. Louis Cardinal said he's suffered hand fractures before and that this felt the same way. He'll be sent for imaging and further tests to determine the true extent.
Contreras has been hit a total of 24 times this season, the third-most in baseball. He seems frustrated, too, saying that it will keep happening "if nobody does anything about it." Sounds like he's frustrated that Boston pitchers haven't come to his defense, threatening to cause an issue for the Red Sox even if his hand injury proves to be nothing serious.
That's not the end of the problems for the Red Sox. Roman Anthony, who missed nearly four months due to a torn finger ligament, is slumping hard. After an initial burst in his first two games back after being activated on August 30, Anthony has slashed just .200/.268/.338 thus far in September.
The biggest news of all, though, is Chapman. If he avoids the IL but is diminished, it could give the Yankees a key advantage in the most crucial moments of the expected matchup. The Sox's other primary bullpen lefty, Erik Miller, is also suffering from mechanical issues at a particularly brutal time. Capitalizing on that edge will be a must, and if the Red Sox fall to New York due to a Chapman postseason meltdown, the moment will be that much sweeter.

ARLINGTON, Texas — When Trevor Story hit his clutch three-run homer to flip a two-run deficit into a one-run lead Thursday against the Rangers, interim manager Chad Tracy didn’t rush to get his two highest-leverage bullpen arms instantly ready. That’s because one of them was unavailable due to a nagging — and previously undisclosed — injury.
With Boston suddenly up, 4-3, Tracy used a pair of rookies (righty Wyatt Olds and lefty Alec Gamboa) to pitch the eighth, then turned things over to righty Garrett Whitlock in the ninth. For at least one night, Whitlock took the job of closer Aroldis Chapman, who has a tight lat muscle.
“He’s just dealing with some lat tightness we’re going to be conservative with,” Tracy said. “It’s getting better, but we’ve got to make sure it gets there. That’s why he wasn’t available tonight.”
Tracy said Chapman — who last pitched Saturday against the Royals — has been dealing with the injury for “a couple of days.” Asked if an injured list stint was possible for the All-Star, Tracy said: “We’re not doing that right now.”
“We’re just going to keep monitoring it and see where he’s at each day,” Tracy said. “Obviously, you know how diligent he is about his prep and getting in and getting treatment, so we’re just monitoring day-to-day.”
Chapman, 38, has had another stellar season in Boston, tallying 34 saves to go along with a 1.95 ERA and 68 strikeouts in 50 ⅔ innings over 52 games. He was one of two key Red Sox players with an injury concern Thursday; first baseman Willson Contreras left the game in the eighth inning after being hit on top of his right hand with a pitch.
Olds, who has a 1.23 ERA and 19 strikeouts in his first 12 MLB appearances since debuting last month, relieved Sonny Gray with one out in the seventh inning and the Sox trailing by two. He got two quick outs before Story’s three-run blast put Boston up 4-3. Olds got Ezequiel Duran to pop out to start the eighth before Gamboa entered for the left-on-left matchup against Corey Seager. Seager singled but Gamboa got Josh Jung to ground into an inning-ending double play five pitches later.
“They were awesome,” Tracy said. “Getting thrust into a big spot, going back out anyways, and then all of the sudden you’re going out with a lead. They did an amazing job.”
Whitlock then recorded his fourth save of the year, needing 12 pitches and getting a similar 6-4-3 double play to end the game.
“He’s great,” Tracy said. “He’s reliable. He’s done it before if Chappy’s down.”

This is why we watch! Trevor Story's season looked dead and buried both three months and three weeks ago. He's battled injury, surgery, rehab, way too many strikeouts, and growing chatter from knuckleheads like me who have repeatedly questioned if he even belongs back in this lineup.
Well tonight, he came to the plate with the Sox down 3-1 in the eighth and on the verge of getting swept. He was facing a tough reliever in Jacob Latz, a Texas team that was 63-1 when leading after seven innings, and the weight of his team going a combined 0-17 with runners in scoring position in the series up to that point.
Then he did this:
As somebody that's been leading the "Trevor Story is cooked " charges, I love this so much! Nothing can humble and amaze quite like baseball, and after months of hard work, grinding behind the scenes, and having to deal with all the noise, Story smashed a 108mph line drive home run not only in the face of Latz and Texas' playoff hopes, but also in the face of all those who have been doubting him for weeks (hand raised).
It's just one game, and the real test doesn't start until the 29th, but boy did this have to feel incredible for Story who hadn't gone deep since May 13th. To do it in that moment, in his home town, and against the backdrop of everything that's happened this year is just so perfectly baseball. It's why we love this game so much, and why people like Story are willing to put in the work behind the scenes for months on end to get the chance to do something amazing like that.
I know some of you might not believe it after what I've written about him in recent weeks, but I truly am very happy for Story! He deserves all the credit tonight!
Oh, and in addition to Story's game changing three-run homer, he followed that up by starting double plays on defense to end both the eighth and ninth:
Baseball really is the best!
Studs
Trevor Story: If I didn't put him here, I'd have to legally resign from Over The Monster.
Wilyer Abreu: He looked a little better tonight with a sharp single in the fourth and a walk that turned into a run on Story's three-run shot.
The bullpen: The comeback wouldn't be complete without the pen holding it down, and with Aroldis Chapman unavailable with lat tightness, Wyatt Olds, Alec Gamboa, and Garrett Whitlock combined to go 2.2 scoreless innings.
Duds
Only one dud tonight, and that's me given my recent stance on Story's playing time. The crow is delicious, and I hope it remains on the menu well into October!
One other important note
Just before Story's home run, Willson Contreras was hit in the hand by a pitch and had to leave the game. The good news is x-rays were negative, but given x-rays were also negative after Curtis Mead got hit in July, I'm not going to be celebrating this one until we get further confirmation.
X-rays were negative on Willson Contreras, at least initially, but he remains sore.
Aroldis Chapman was unavailable due to lat tightness and is day-to-day.

This has been a rough stretch for the Red Sox offense, which has effectively turned into a pumpkin after a torrid two months this summer. This week in particular the bats have fallen silent, and for much of Thursday night the Red Sox looked like they were headed toward a discouraging series sweep at the worst possible time.
Things took an especially grim turn when Willson Contreras left the game in the eighth inning after being hit in the hand by a pitch, but while the specter of his absence will loom over the club in the days to come, Trevor Story once again proved that you can never count this Red Sox team out.
The veteran shortstop came through with a go-ahead three-run home run in the top of the eighth inning, flipping the script and giving the Red Sox a badly needed 4-3 win to avoid a sweep at the hands of the Texas Rangers.
Story’s shot came with one out against Rangers closer Jacob Latz, completing a three-run comeback and cutting Boston’s magic number to clinch a playoff spot to three with nine games remaining.
“To steal that last one is huge,” Story told NESN’s Jahmai Webster postgame. “It’s momentum we can ride out into Tampa.”
Prior to Story’s home run, Thursday was shaping up to be among the club’s worst losses of the season.
A hallmark of the offense’s struggles early in the year was a lot of empty, uncompetitive at-bats, tons of swing and miss and a general inability to make good contact. Even with the Rangers opting for a bullpen game led by Cody Bradford, whose fastball averages just 88.6 mph, the Red Sox couldn’t square anything up.
The Red Sox only managed two hits through the first five innings, both singles in the fourth inning. That put runners at the corners with two outs, but Jarren Duran grounded out to squander the opportunity.
It was a similar story in the sixth, when Wilyer Abreu singled and Adley Rutschman finally did some damage with a ground-rule double into the left-field gap. Had the ball stayed in play, Abreu probably would have scored, but instead the Red Sox had two men in scoring position for Story, who worked a full count and struck out to end the threat.
The offense did nothing to pick up Sonny Gray, who wasn’t perfect but did everything he could to keep the Red Sox in the game.
The veteran right-hander allowed a solo home run to Josh Jung with two outs in the first, and in the second he walked the first two batters of the inning, both of whom came around to score on an RBI bloop single by Danny Jansen and a run-scoring squeeze bunt by Evan Carter.
Gray settled down afterward and retired 14 of the last 16 batters he faced from the second inning into the seventh. He was charged with three runs over 6 1/3 innings and limited the Rangers to three hits and three walks with six strikeouts.
“I thought he was awesome,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said. “The only blemish was the two walks, we kind of walked ourselves into the part of their lineup where they can play baseball a little bit with bunts and they drop a flare into center and there’s a safety squeeze, outside of that, that was a really, really good effort.”
Even when the Red Sox finally scored in the top of the seventh, they did so without recording a hit. Nate Eaton and Caleb Durbin led off with consecutive walks and Eaton advanced to third after Nick Sogard hit a rocket of a fly out to the center field wall. But with one out and a chance to fight back into the game, Roman Anthony grounded into a run-scoring fielder’s choice to make it 3-1. He advanced to second after the Rangers threw away the double-play attempt, but Mickey Gasper grounded out to end the inning.
Then came the eighth.
Once again the Red Sox got two men on base right away, with Abreu drawing a leadoff walk before Contreras was hit in the right hand by a pitch. He immediately left the game with the trainer and was replaced at first by Isiah Kiner-Falefa, but while the Red Sox worried about their slugger, the Rangers pulled Jakob Junis for their closer Latz, who has been among the most dominant closers in the American League this year.
Latz drew a pop out from Rutschman, but then Story stepped up to the plate and everything changed.
“You see one of our guys keeled over holding his hand and you’re down in the dumps seeing that and moments later the whole dugout erupts,” Tracy said. “We haven’t been doing much offensively for a few days and to get a swing right there and feel like you steal a game, it was enormous. Big emotion swing.”
With the lead in hand, Wyatt Olds and Alec Gamboa pitched a scoreless eighth, and with Aroldis Chapman unavailable, Garrett Whitlock came on for the ninth and locked down the save for the win. Story and Sogard turned inning-ending double plays in both the eighth and the ninth to ensure the Rangers couldn’t mount one last comeback.
“Good teams find a way to win and we’ve been doing that in the second half and that’s kind of who you become,” Story said. “And you feel that momentum, you feel that vibe around the game and we never give up.”
X-rays negative, Chapman day-to-day
The Red Sox got some good news postgame when X-rays on Contreras’ hand came back negative.
“He’s got a bruise on the hand and some swelling,” Tracy said. “So we’ll just take it day to day and see how he is.”
Tracy also confirmed that Chapman has been dealing with some lat tightness for the past few days and they are taking a conservative approach.
“It’s getting better but have to make sure it gets there, that’s why he wasn’t available tonight,” Tracy said, adding that an IL stint isn’t being considered for Chapman right now.

Video Transcript
What's up, everyone?
Zach Coe here for Roundtable.
Ahead of Tuesday night's loss to the Rangers, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters that reliever Justin Slayton's season was over after an orthopedic visit revealed degenerative changes in his flexor mass, which required a PRP injection, effectively ending his season.
So obviously, the Red Sox have one of the best bullpens in baseball, backend of Aroldis Chapman, Justin Slayton, and Tayron Guerrero when he returns from the injured list.
But the loss of Slayton is still a really big one for this Red Sox bullpen, especially in the postseason when managers tend to be more aggressive with the hooks on both starters and relievers.
It was a pretty underwhelming season for Slayton when you look at the final line.
It was a 4.60 ERA in 31 1/3 innings.
But he was prone to a couple blowup starts, and that really inflated his ERA for much of the season.
It'll be interesting to see how Tracy's able to piece together the bullpen in Slayton's absence.
Of course, like I said, you have the backend pretty solidified with Tayron Guerrero handling the seventh, Garrett Whitlock in the eighth to All-Star Aroldis Chapman, who's been one of the best closers in baseball over the last two seasons.
But it's how you get to them that I really have some concerns about, and there are plenty of guys that are available to fill that role, but it's whether or not they'll be able to capitalize on their opportunities.
First one being Greg Weiser.
I wrote about it a little bit earlier, but ever since he was recalled from his brief demotion to Triple-A, he's been incredible for the Red Sox, stepping up as they lost guys like Whitlock to an IL stint, Slayton, who landed on the IL shortly after Whitlock, and most recently Guerrero.
There's also Tanner Houk, who's working his way back from Tommy John surgery he underwent last year.
He's gonna try to make a return in a bullpen capacity for the last week of the season.
And then there's the big wild card of it all in Garrett Crochet, who continues to throw side sessions as he tries to get back in a relief role for the postseason.
He's been on the injured list since April 29th with left shoulder inflammation.
So any of those guys are more than capable of stepping up and filling that role.
It's just gonna be about whether or not they're, one, healthy enough to go out there and throw on a near nightly basis like the team might need them to in the postseason, and two, whether or not they're gonna be productive enough.
Obviously, with Houk, he's coming back from Tommy John surgery, and typically you see guys be a little bit wild with their control when they first come back from Tommy John.
We saw it in Houk's first relea-- We saw it in his first rehab appearance with Portland.
He walked two guys, and a run scored as a result.
But it's been a little bit better, since then in the two appearances following that.
So we'll see if that is something that he can shake.
And then Crochet, he's just We haven't seen him in so long, it's tough to say whether or not he's gonna be as effective as he once was.
And even if he isn't able to get to the 2025 Cy Young runner-up caliber, can he at least give you enough to kind of bridge that gap between the starter and to the backend of your bullpen?
And then there's kind of a wild card in it all, and a bit of a forgotten man in Johan Oviedo, who obviously has electric stuff, but he's made only one appearance in a Red Sox uniform before landing on the IL with right elbow inflammation.
So he's planning on making a rehab appearance with Triple-A Worcester on Thursday night, and then they'll figure out the next steps with him.
But Red Sox have plenty of options to fill that void left behind by Slayton.

item.content:encoded:
RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses the potential relievers who could step up and fill the void left behind by Justin Slaten after it was revealed the right-hander was unlikely to return from the injured list in 2026. Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
After an incredible July that saw the Boston Red Sox go 21-4, ultimately saving their season and propelling them into postseason position, the team has given key contributors time on the injured list to address lingering injuries. Among the players placed on the IL was right-handed reliever Justin Slaten, who was dealing with right elbow soreness.
After initially expecting to miss the minimum of 15 days or somewhere close to it, the 29-year-old continued to experience soreness as he began throwing progressions, leading the team to shut him down each time. On Tuesday, interim manager Chad Tracy announced that Slaten received a PRP injection to treat "degenerative changes in his flexor mass," ending his season.
With Slaten set to miss the remainder of the year, the pressure is on these pitchers to help bridge the gap between the starter and All-Star closer Aroldis Chapman:
Tyron Guerrero
Guerrero was expected to be activated off the injured list ahead of Wednesday night's loss to the Texas Rangers, but tightness in his lower back led the team to delay his activation. Still, though, upon his activation, Guerrero will become one of the primary seventh-inning options for Tracy to turn to.
The 35-year-old flamethrower has been an incredible find for Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow, posting a 3.26 ERA in 38.2 innings in 2026. However, he hit a rough patch before landing on the IL, allowing eight earned runs in his last 13.2 innings. Boston will need him to return to the pitcher he was for the first 38.2 innings of his season, when he posted a 2.16 ERA.
After not allowing a single earned run in his first 10 appearances after being dealt to Boston at the trade deadline, the 28-year-old lefty has struggled in his last six outings, allowing five earned runs, including three in a blow-up appearance in Wednesday's loss.
Miller told reporters after the loss that he was working through a mechanical issue that led to the struggles. However, he is the primary left-handed high-leverage arm before Chapman, so the team will need him to get those issues squared away ahead of what's likely to be a Wild Card-round matchup against a New York Yankees lineup that's lefty-heavy.
No single pitcher has stepped up more for the Red Sox as they shuffled Garrett Whitlock, Slaten, and Guerrero on the injured list than Weissert. After a brief demotion to Triple-A Worcester on Aug. 7, Weissert returned to the big leagues on Aug. 13, taking Whitlock's spot on the active roster, and has been lights out ever since. In 10.2 innings since being recalled, the 31-year-old right-hander has allowed only two earned runs on 12 hits, striking out 14 and walking only four.
Weissert figures to be the leader in the clubhouse to take over Slaten's role in the bullpen.
A trio of injured options
The Red Sox have several pitchers looking to return from the injured list before the end of the regular season who could factor into the team's playoff push, including 2025 Cy Young Award runner-up Garrett Crochet, 2024 All-Star Tanner Houck, and Johan Oviedo.
Crochet
The 27-year-old ace has thrown four bullpen sessions since restarting a throwing progression on Aug. 3, with his most recent outing, a 30-pitch up-and-down session on the Fenway Park mound, coming on Tuesday afternoon. While Crochet, if healthy enough to appear in games, will almost certainly be on the postseason roster, he is expected to make multi-inning appearances rather than one-inning spurts like Slaten had been used, making him a valuable weapon but an imperfect replacement.
Houck
The now-30-year-old right-hander is attempting to return to the Boston staff in a "Swiss Army knife" role after undergoing Tommy John surgery in August 2025. Houck has already made three rehab appearances with both Double-A Portland and Triple-A Worcester, allowing two earned runs on one hit, walking four, and striking out seven in 4.2 innings. He is expected to return to Worcester on Saturday for a 40-50 pitch outing before potentially rejoining the Red Sox.
Though what exactly Houck can contribute after being out of major league action since May 2025 remains to be seen.
Oviedo
A bit of a forgotten man in the 2026 Red Sox season is the 28-year-old right-hander, who made only one appearance before landing on the injured list on April 3 with right elbow inflammation. Oviedo will make his first rehab appearance Thursday night with Worcester before deciding on next steps; at this point, the risk likely outweighs the reward of making the postseason roster.
Tracy, Breslow, and the rest of Boston's decision makers will have 10 games to make their final decisions on how exactly the postseason roster will look, and who will replace Slaten's high-leverage innings.
Up next for the Sox
The Red Sox will look to avoid the sweep at the hands of the Texas Rangers in Thursday's series finale from Globe Life Field. Sonny Gray (17-5, 2.76 ERA) gets the start for Boston opposite Tyler Alexander (5-2, 3.38 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are still sitting comfortably in the second Wild Card spot, but there are several issues they must resolve before they start thinking about playoff baseball.
Boston is a mediocre 11-11 over its last 22 games. While that's been good enough to sustain its playoff position, its play hasn't exactly inspired optimism for a deep postseason run.
Most of the Red Sox' problems can be linked to their underperforming lineup. Key hitters like Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman and Wilyer Abreu have been concerningly inconsistent.
A deeper dive into the numbers suggests the struggling Sox will have their work cut out for them in their presumed Wild Card Series rematch at Yankee Stadium. Here are the club's five biggest areas of concern with 10 games remaining:
Roman Anthony is ice-cold
The Red Sox need Roman Anthony to be one of their best offensive players to have any chance of a deep postseason run. If the former No. 1 prospect continues to play the way he has for most of September, that will be problematic.
Anthony is hitting just .149 (7-for-47) with one home run and a .428 OPS over his last 11 games. He has struck out 18 times in 51 plate appearances.
The 22-year-old's struggles beg the question: should he still be the leadoff hitter in the postseason? Interim manager Chad Tracy will have no choice but to reevaluate Anthony's spot in the lineup if his woes continue. The problem with that is there aren't any exciting alternatives. The leadoff spot has been a glaring issue all season long, regardless of who has been thrust into the role.
Struggling against high velocity
The Red Sox offense has been inconsistent no matter who's on the mound, but it has mostly struggled against pitchers with high velo. Here's how some of Boston's regulars have fared this season against pitches greater than or equal to 97 mph:
- Wilyer Abreu: .170 BA, .623 OPS (237 pitches)
- Jarren Duran: .065 BA, .300 OPS (203 pitches)
- Willson Contreras: .170 BA, .512 OPS (166 pitches)
- Ceddanne Rafaela: .205 BA, .449 OPS (157 pitches)
- Roman Anthony: .091 BA, .440 OPS (58 pitches)
- Adley Rutschman: .077 BA, .451 OPS (57 pitches)
The Red Sox' top performer against high velocity (97 mph and above) has been Caleb Durbin (.364 BA, .912 OPS, 161 pitches).
Being so vulnerable against high velocity will especially be a problem for Boston in its expected Wild Card Series matchup against the New York Yankees. Cy Young frontrunner and likely Game 1 starter Cam Schlittler averages 98 mph with his four-seam fastball, which he uses 44.5 percent of the time. Gerrit Cole averages 96.9 mph with his four-seam, using it 49.3 percent of the time.
Leaving runners stranded
Boston has been below average all season at capitalizing on runners in scoring position. It currently ranks 17th in batting average (.250) and 21st in OPS (.731) with RISP. They're hitting just .212 in such situations through 14 games so far in September.
The Yankees' elite pitching staff probably won't provide the Red Sox with many scoring opportunities in their short series, so it's imperative that they come through when given the chance. Lately, Boston hasn't had anyone in its lineup to feel confident about when they step to the plate with runners on.
Role players regressing
As great as guys like Willson Contreras, Caleb Durbin, and Wilyer Abreu were throughout the Red Sox' incredible midseason turnaround, it was the role players who powered their surge. Mickey Gasper, Jahmai Jones, Nick Sogard, Anthony Seigler, and Andruw Monasterio were instrumental in resurrecting Boston's season.
Gasper has cooled off, though no one expected him to sustain his Barry Bonds-like run. Jahmai Jones is 4 for his last 22 (.182) with nine strikeouts, suddenly making him a playoff roster cut candidate. Sogard is still hitting, but his .758 OPS so far in September suggests regression to the mean. Seigler is hurt. Monasterio posted a .578 OPS in August and is 0-for-11 so far in September, putting him on the playoff roster bubble.
That group deserves immense credit for getting the Red Sox here, but it cannot be counted on to propel the club through the postseason.
Erik Miller experiencing command issues
Boston's bullpen is arguably its biggest strength heading into the postseason. The back end with Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, and Aroldis Chapman is elite.
We would've included trade deadline addition Erik Miller in that group last month, when he allowed only one earned run with 20 strikeouts and just three walks across his first 11 appearances with the Red Sox. His performance so far this month, however, has been alarming.
Miller, acquired from the San Francisco Giants in the Marcelo Mayer trade, has allowed four earned runs with six walks and six strikeouts through five appearances (4.1 IP) in September. His command struggles were a question mark upon his joining the club, and it appears that issue has reemerged with less than two weeks until the playoffs.
After Wednesday's poor outing against the Texas Rangers (2 H, 3 ER, 1 BB), Miller attributed his recent struggles to his mechanics. The Red Sox will hope that whatever the problem is, it's a quick fix, because Miller will be counted on to be their most reliable left-handed reliever not named Aroldis Chapman.

Good morning! Last night, Jake Bennett was unable to hold the Rangers in check during the team's 7-3 loss in Texas. Some of his numbers look good (seven strikeouts against just one walk), but he also surrendered eight hits in just 4.2 innings, which did in his evening.
With just ten games left in the season, the question now becomes how should the Sox use Bennett going forward? With some combination of Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle and Ranger Suarez likely to get lined up in a best of three Wild Card Series, do you just hold Bennett on the sidelines and hope he gets to come back into the fold as a fourth starter in the ALDS or even ALCS? Or do you start transitioning him to some sort of relief role?
It's a bit of an awkward moment for Bennett. He's been getting knocked around during his last two outings while Suarez is seemingly getting locked in. It almost certainly cuts him out of the Wild Card rotation, and if the Sox get some combination of Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck and Tyron Guerrero back to add to Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock and Erik Miller in the bullpen, Bennett largely gets squeezed out of relevance.
So how do you want him used? Do those six shutout innings Bennett threw against the Yankees back on August 29th make you want the Sox to find a role for him if they play New York? Do you think he's just a young pitcher who looks out of gas and want to hide him until the team needs a fourth starter?
Use this space to talk about Bennett and the rest of the difficult upcoming pitching staff decisions, and, as always, be good to one another.

When the Boston Red Sox sent former top-prospect Marcelo Mayer to the San Francisco Giants for Erik Miller, CBO Craig Breslow was sending a major signal. This season is about winning, and Miller will be more help with that now.
For a while, the hard-throwing lefty has been exactly that. A major spark out of the bullpen who makes the Red Sox incredibly intimidating on the mound in the late innings. In his first 14 appearances with Boston, Miller gave up just two runs.
The last two games have been more of a struggle for Miller, though. In 1.1 innings, he’s given up four runs. That includes three runs in Wednesday’s rough loss to the Texas Rangers, which was good enough for Miller to earn a loss.
Boston Red Sox RP Erik Miller Opened Up on Struggles
Following Wednesday’s loss, Erik Miller faced the media following the game. There, he explained that his main issue on Wednesday was that he had control issues. Those control issues put him in bad counts, which made him predictable.
“Just not doing what I’ve been doing well,” Erik Miller said. “Just not getting ahead of guys. Getting behind. Falling into hitters’ counts… Guy knows what’s coming, it usually doesn’t end well. Just kind of working through some stuff right now.”
Red Sox fans and media both noticed Miller saying that he’s working through some stuff. Luckily, that doesn’t mean an injury. It’s more a reference to letting his mechanics get away from him.
“Yeah. Some stuff I’m trying to clean up a little. At some point throughout the year, stuff crops up. You’ve been doing really well and some bad habits kind of come up. So, I’ve just got to work through it. Get back to what I was doing and go from there,” Miller said.
The Red Sox need the version of Miller they’ve largely gotten since the trade. He has a 2.87 ERA in Boston, to go along with a 1.277 WHIP and 14.9 strikeouts per nine. That’s in 15.2 innings over 16 appearances.
Garrett Crochet Will Return to the Red Sox as a Reliever
The Red Sox bullpen is set to get a major boost soon. Ace pitcher Garrett Crochet is getting ready to make his return, but it won’t be as a starter. It’ll be as another power lefty for the bullpen to use.
The expectation had been that Crochet won’t be able to make a rehab and would jump back in right as the first-round of the playoffs start. That may not be the case now. It was recently reported that he could be ready even sooner. That means he’ll potentially pitch in the regular season as a kind of rehab.
“The comebacks of potential October contributors like Tanner Houck, Garrett Crochet, Johan Oviedo and others might also be aided by the fact the Red Sox might have a week (or more) to set up for the postseason,” Chris Cotillo of MassLive wrote. “It’s not out of the question that the club has someone like Crochet pitch in one of the final regular season games of the year in what’s effectively a rehab outing at the major league level in a game that matters little in the standings.”
It’s excellent news for the Red Sox. With Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, a healthy Garrett Crochet, and Erik Miller, Boston can feel very confident if they get just five innings from a starter.
